title.analysis: Who Can Actually Afford a $750K House in 2026? (SHOCKING Math). The 69-character title combines a concrete price and year with an eligibility question and an all-caps emotional promise. It addresses search intent for the income needed to buy a $750,000 home and browse interest in exclusion from homeownership. The script supplies a detailed illustrative cost stack, but 'who can afford' cannot be answered nationally without location, down payment, debts, household size, taxes, insurance, loan program and comfort criteria. 'SHOCKING' is subjective, and the script's categorical $260,000 boundary exceeds what its own assumption-sensitive model can establish.
title.script_alignment: The $750,000 calculation is delivered immediately and revisited throughout. The title is directionally fulfilled, but the script turns one 10%-down scenario into a national eligibility rule and mixes underwriting ratios with discretionary comfort.

thumbnail.analysis: Actual 1280x720 white thumbnail: worried cartoon man at left, thick arrow, large black '$750K... WHO?' and a suburban house bound in red chains. The price and WHO remain immediately legible at 320x180; the chain metaphor survives but house detail becomes secondary. It complements the title with exclusion and entrapment rather than adding a second calculation. The image makes unaffordability categorical even though the script ultimately presents conditional affordability for a narrow high-income case. Historical artwork, impressions, CTR and thumbnail tests are unavailable.

script.opening_words: A real estate agent handed me a flyer last weekend at an open house. Glossy, folded in thirds, smelled faintly of toner. The headline across the top said, Your starter home awaits.
script.ending_words: Run your own numbers. Be honest about what you see. And if the math doesn't work, that's not you failing the system. That's the system telling you the truth.

script.analysis: The script uses sensory specificity, escalating calculations, an illustrative couple and shame-relief permission to make affordability emotionally concrete. The core 10%-down mortgage arithmetic is close and the cost-stack addition is internally correct. It also clearly distinguishes approval from living comfortably in parts of the narrative. Credibility weakens when anecdotes are presented as market medians without receipts, a single national model is generalized across jurisdictions, non-comparable survey populations are combined, and forecasts or universal statements replace bounded assumptions. The Bennett expense list sums to about a $2,695 monthly deficit, not exactly $3,000. The ending returns to a defensible instruction—run household-specific numbers—but only after several unsupported categorical claims. No audio, edit, delivery, timing or on-screen evidence was inspected.

claim_audit.claim: A 20% down payment is $150,000; 10% down leaves a $675,000 loan; $4,177 monthly principal and interest at 6.3%
claim_audit.assessment: Arithmetic reproduces: 20% of $750,000 is $150,000, 10% is $75,000 and the loan is $675,000. A 30-year 6.30% fixed amortization is about $4,178 monthly, consistent with the script. Freddie Mac reported a 6.30% weekly average on 2026-04-30; an individual quote varies by borrower and fees.

claim_audit.claim: Median household transaction accounts are about $8,000
claim_audit.assessment: Supported only with a vintage and population boundary: the 2022 Survey of Consumer Finances reports a $8,000 median among families holding transaction accounts in 2022 dollars. It is not a 2026 savings-account balance and does not describe every prospective buyer.

claim_audit.claim: Saving 15% of median income produces $12,500 annually and needs 12 years for $150,000
claim_audit.assessment: $12,500 times 12 equals $150,000 and implies income near $83,333. The calculation ignores returns, taxes, existing savings, closing costs and price changes. 'Almost no one' saves 15% and prices 'will' rise are unsupported absolutes.

claim_audit.claim: First-time buyers are age 40, only 21% of buyers, and almost a quarter receive family gifts
claim_audit.assessment: NAR's 2025 survey of successful primary-residence buyers supports median age 40, first-time share 21% and gifts or loans from family/friends for 22% of first-time buyers. It does not describe all households trying to buy, and it does not support the generational claim that grandparents owned two houses by 40.

claim_audit.claim: PMI persists until 78% of original value and takes roughly nine years
claim_audit.assessment: Federal law generally requires automatic termination at scheduled 78% original value if current, while borrower-requested cancellation may occur at 80% subject to conditions. Duration depends on rate, term, amortization, extra payments, refinancing and loan type; nine years is not universal.

claim_audit.claim: The cost stack is $6,045 monthly and implies $259,000 at 28% or $201,000 at 36%
claim_audit.assessment: $4,177+$563+$400+$625+$280=$6,045. Annualizing and dividing by 28% gives $259,071; dividing by 36% gives $201,500. But 36% is a total-debt ratio, not a housing-only comfort rule, and maintenance is not normally a mortgage-underwriting payment. Taxes, insurance and PMI vary materially.

claim_audit.claim: Only 12%-13% of U.S. households earn $200,000 or more
claim_audit.assessment: The 2024 ACS S1901 estimate is 15.6% of households at $200,000 or more. The script understates the share and then equates income membership with ability to afford one scenario, ignoring wealth, equity, debts and geography.

claim_audit.claim: The Bennett household is $3,000 per month in the red
claim_audit.assessment: Using the script's figures, non-housing expenses total $7,850; adding $6,045 housing to $11,200 take-home yields a $2,695 deficit. 'About $3,000' is reasonable rounding, but take-home pay, childcare and every expense are illustrative and not an authenticated household.

claim_audit.claim: A Goldman Sachs survey found 40% of people earning $300,000-$500,000 live paycheck to paycheck
claim_audit.assessment: The located 2025 Goldman Sachs Retirement Survey says roughly 40% of working Americans report living paycheck to paycheck. It does not support the transcript's $300,000-$500,000 income-specific statistic. The attribution is therefore unsupported as stated.

claim_audit.claim: Mortgage delinquencies hit 11.5%, highest since 2021; 2022-2023 vintages perform worst
claim_audit.assessment: The statement omits a denominator and loan class. ICE reported a national delinquency rate of 3.42% in September 2025 and separately elevated FHA delinquency near 11%; an FHA-specific rate cannot be labeled all mortgages. No primary receipt located here establishes the asserted worst origination vintages.

claim_audit.claim: Q1 2026 foreclosure starts rose 20% and bank repossessions 45% year over year
claim_audit.assessment: ATTOM's 2026 Q1 report supports both year-over-year changes and 14,020 repossessions. ATTOM is the originating property-data provider, not a government series. Rising activity does not establish that $750,000 buyers or 2022-2023 loans caused the increase.

claim_audit.claim: $150,000 invested grows to $2.6 million in 30 years, plus $4.5 million from the monthly difference
claim_audit.assessment: $150,000 compounded annually at exactly 10% becomes about $2.617 million before taxes, fees and volatility. The $4.5 million claim omits the assumed monthly contribution and return: it requires about $1,991 per month at 10% or $3,689 at 7%. Historical averages are not guaranteed; rent, ownership costs, home appreciation, transaction costs and tax treatment must be modeled consistently.

claim_audit.claim: Grandparents bought at twice income, parents at three times, and viewers face nine times income; a physician cannot buy in half the country
claim_audit.assessment: No population, year, geography, price series, income denominator or physician earnings distribution is cited. These rhetorical comparisons are not reproducible and should not be treated as national facts.

topic.analysis: The topic is the cash-flow affordability of a $750,000 U.S. home under a 10%-down, 30-year fixed-rate scenario. The intended audience is middle- and upper-middle-income viewers confronting high-cost markets or seeking permission not to buy. A rigorous version should offer a state- and household-adjustable range rather than a single national salary gate, separate lender qualification from a household comfort budget, and compare renting versus owning under disclosed return, appreciation and tenure assumptions.
topic.audience_problem: Prospective buyers need a full, location-specific ownership budget and a clear separation between mortgage approval, emergency resilience and comfortable discretionary cash flow.
topic.novelty_and_corpus_angle: Build an interactive affordability matrix across down payments, current rate, state tax/insurance, other debts and target savings buffer. Show underwriting and comfort thresholds separately, plus rent-invest and buy scenarios with sensitivity bands instead of one forecast.
topic.competition: Frozen performance is 0.56895x TYPICAL against ten peers but 0.49967x WEAK against five. A closely related $500K affordability video was a strong historical counterexample, while nearby housing videos were typical, so the topic/price formula is not uniformly predictive.

virality.analysis: The frozen result is 6,828 views, 208 likes and 72 comments at 130.1484 days: 52.46319 views/day, 0.56895x TYPICAL against ten peers and 0.49967x WEAK against five. The concrete price, eligibility question and legible chained-house image create immediate comprehension, but the tier changes at the threshold when the peer frame narrows. The same channel's $500K affordability video is a strong counterexample, while 'When Should The Average American Buy A House?' and 'Why Buying A House In 2026 Is A Financial Trap' are typical. This supports cohort sensitivity and rejects a simple causal claim about the packaging formula.

original_content_lesson.test: Compare a household-specific affordability calculator title/thumbnail with the categorical WHO framing, holding presenter, price point and release window constant. Disclose rate, down payment and state assumptions; measure owned CTR, first-minute retention, calculator completion and correction feedback.
original_content_lesson.confidence: HIGH for text/image integrity, arithmetic reproduction and frozen cohorts; MEDIUM for audience and topic interpretation; LOW for causal performance explanation.

event.linkage: Publication followed Freddie Mac's 6.30% weekly rate observation by three days and ATTOM's Q1 foreclosure report by seventeen days. Primary sources support the mortgage-rate, first-time-buyer and transaction-account context, but several nationalized eligibility and stress claims are unsupported or mis-scoped.
